title: A simple overflow density separation method for recovering dense microplastics from sediment
author: Crutchett, Bornt

steps.title: Add sediment and initial rinse
steps.instruction: Add approximately 10 g of sediment to a 50 mL Erlenmeyer flask. Rinse the inside of the flask with ≤ 25 mL ZnCl₂ from the wash bottle to wash down any adhering particles.

steps.title: First agitation and spatula rinse
steps.instruction: Using a spatula (or similar), thoroughly agitate the sample for one minute with a gentle, non‑uniform motion to avoid vortex formation. After agitation, remove the spatula and rinse it with a small amount of ZnCl₂, returning any adhering particles to the flask.

steps.title: Transfer flask to beaker
steps.instruction: Lift the Erlenmeyer flask, rinse its outside with filtered water, and place it inside a 400 mL glass beaker.

steps.title: Fill flask to neck and second agitation
steps.instruction: Fill the Erlenmeyer flask with additional ZnCl₂ up to the base of the neck while disturbing any particles caught in surface tension. Perform a second agitation with the spatula as described above, being careful not to rinse the spatula excessively; if too much ZnCl₂ is already present, rinse the spatula into the overflow beaker instead.

steps.title: Adjust ZnCl₂ level and wait
steps.instruction: If needed, add ZnCl₂ to a level 1 cm below the top of the flask; a few drops may be added to disperse surface sediment particles shortly after agitation. Allow the suspension to stand for at least 20 min (or longer, depending on solution clarity) for particles to separate before proceeding.

steps.title: First overflow pour
steps.instruction: Ensure the bottom of the Erlenmeyer flask touches one wall of the beaker. Submerge the tip of a funnel approximately 1 cm into the supernatant, position the tip away from the edge that will overflow, and gently pour 15 mL ZnCl₂ at ~1 mL · s⁻¹. If the liquid is poured too quickly or the funnel is too low, pause until settled material resettles.

steps.title: Rinse funnel after first pour
steps.instruction: Remove the funnel tip from the solution and rinse it with ZnCl₂ to wash any adhering particles into the overflow beaker.

steps.title: Tilt beaker to overflow supernatant
steps.instruction: Gently tilt the beaker until the top edge of the Erlenmeyer flask contacts the inside wall, then allow approximately 2 cm of supernatant to overflow into the beaker. If settled particles are disturbed, stop tilting and let the contents resettle before retrying.

steps.title: Second overflow after agitation
steps.instruction: Conduct another agitation of the flask, allow the solution to settle as before, and then collect a second overflow using the same tilt method.

steps.title: Rinse top half of flask
steps.instruction: While the flask remains in the beaker, rinse the outside top half of the Erlenmeyer flask with ZnCl₂, taking care not to fill the flask and cause another overflow. Pay special attention to the rim to remove any adhering particles.

steps.title: Rinse bottom half and collect float
steps.instruction: Raise the Erlenmeyer flask out of the overflow solution and rinse the outside bottom half of the glass into the overflow beaker with ZnCl₂. The overflow beaker now contains the “float” fraction for subsequent filtration.

steps.title: Set aside sink fraction flask
steps.instruction: Place the Erlenmeyer flask, now containing the “sink” fraction, aside for later filtration.

steps.title: Filter float fraction onto 25 mm filter
steps.instruction: Under vacuum, pour the contents of the overflow beaker onto the centre of a 25 mm diameter stainless‑steel filter at ~1 mL · s⁻¹ to avoid solution buildup on the filter.

steps.title: Rinse overflow beaker and funnel
steps.instruction: Thoroughly rinse the inside of the overflow beaker with filtered H₂O to transfer all float particles into the filtration funnel. Then rinse the funnel with additional filtered H₂O to wash adhered particles onto the filter and remove residual ZnCl₂.

steps.title: Remove funnel and brush particles
steps.instruction: Turn the vacuum off, carefully remove the filtration funnel, and inspect its inner edge for visible particles. Gently brush any particles onto the filter using a fine‑tipped probe, then remove the filter with fine tweezers and place it in a glass Petri dish.

steps.title: Inspect funnel again for missed particles
steps.instruction: Examine the filtration funnel under a stereo microscope and immediately relocate any remaining particles onto the filter to prevent airborne loss.

steps.title: Dry float filter
steps.instruction: Dry the Petri dish containing the filter in an oven set to ≤ 50 °C for 24 h, with the lid offset and covered with aluminium foil, or alternatively enclose the dish in a larger glass Petri dish.

steps.title: Vacuum filter sink fraction onto 47 mm filter
steps.instruction: Vacuum‑filter the Erlenmeyer flask containing the sink fraction onto a 47 mm diameter glass‑fibre filter.

steps.title: Rinse sink filter with filtered water
steps.instruction: Rinse any remaining sediment into the vacuum filtration funnel with filtered H₂O, then thoroughly rinse the filter with filtered H₂O to remove residual ZnCl₂.

steps.title: Dry sink filter
steps.instruction: Remove the sink filter from the vacuum setup, transfer it to a glass Petri dish, and dry it in the same ≤ 50 °C oven for 24 h as described for the float filter.

description: The efficacy of removing microplastics with this overflow density separation method was validated by spiking and then recovering medium and high-density microplastics from sediment. Five replicate density separations were conducted using sediment spiked with visually distinctive microplastics. PA, crumbed rubber (CR), PVC, PET and polyester (PES) 500 µm < 1000 µm in length were used to determine the percent recovery of plastic with increasing densities (Table 1). Polymer densities can broadly vary from manufacturing additives, weathering and biofouling [1]; therefore, density ranges were identified for the spiking polymers (Table 1) by testing their buoyancy in incremental ZnCl2 concentrations (1.00 - 1.60 g cm−3). The number of spiked polymers were counted and verified by two analysts who independently inspected each float filter (Fig. 3c) [6].Table 1Reference polymers used for spiking to validate the overflow density separation method.
